utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Milan Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, good afternoon. On behalf of my client, I would like to point out a fact; namely, duly taking into account all the problems involved in the organisation of these proceedings and the proceedings themselves, and also the gravity of his position and the position of the other accused who came to this building this morning at 8.30 and since then they have been in cells, on their own, for them and for their psychological condition, this is unbearable. They would kindly ask the Honourable Trial Chamber to look into this situation and to prevent this from happening again, namely, from having them brought to the Court building and then not knowing whether Mr. Simic will come or when. So now, after all that time, they have to spend another three or four hours here. They should follow the proceedings. They say that they have certain difficulties with their concentration and things like that. I would kindly like to ask you the following: If there is the possibility - and I believe there is such a possibility - to allow my client to address the Trial Chamber directly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Why? Is there anything you can't speak for him? Because if the problem is what you have expressed, then it is understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's it, basically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Then there's no need for the accused to address the Chamber directly, because this is really an administrative matter. It's unfortunate that this is what happened today. The Trial Chamber was not aware. One would have thought that they would have been taken back, especially after it was decided that the proceedings can't start earlier than 1500 hours. It's unfortunate. The Trial Chamber will see to it that this doesn't happen again, and the Registry assistant will take up the matter with the people responsible for the keeping of the accused here and the transportation, especially in this case, where we have these unusual problems which are not common with other trials.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you also for the efforts that you will make in order to improve their situation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Prosecution still continuing with examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Mr. Salkic, you've told us about the period of time that you were in Batkovic and that you were being kept in some sort of agricultural storage facility there. Is that the place that you were eventually exchanged from?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I want you to turn your attention to the period of time immediately preceding your transfer from Batkovic and your eventual exchange. Firstly, in the period of time shortly before your exchange, did you see any of the defendants at Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I saw -- you see how names can just slip your mind. Brko we called him. Miroslav Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Where were you when you saw him? I know you were at Batkovic, but what were you doing? Were you doing any work, or were you just sitting around as a prisoner? Under what circumstances did you see him?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The first time I saw him in Batkovici, it was a few days before the exchange would actually take place. And I actually was on that list for that exchange. This was probably a preparation for our exchange. I saw him from the yard. There was a barbed-wire fence around the yard, and there were two submachine-guns at two corners that were there in order to prevent anyone from escaping. During the day, you could walk around there a bit. I did not go to work on that day because the proceedings had been initiated against me, so I saw very well when the gentleman went from the car to the office, to the office of this warden of the camp, prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Just -- I'd like to clarify two points that arise from your answer. You say that you were actually on the list for that exchange. On the day that you have just described when you saw Mr. Tadic, did you become aware of your name being included on any list, or did you find out about that at a later stage?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I found that out only later when they called out our names in the morning. They said the names of some persons who were not supposed to go and work that day. Some people went to work; I didn't. They said that we should stay behind. They did not explain to us why they did not call our names out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll get on to the list, then, at a later point. The second matter that I wanted to clarify is that you didn't -- you didn't go to work that day because "the proceedings had been initiated against me." At the time that you saw Mr. Tadic in Batkovic, had the court proceedings in Bijeljina been completed? Or were they still ongoing? Or were you meant to go to Bijeljina that very day? Can you recall?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Actually, they kept us in Bijeljina only for a few hours. Then they brought us to this hangar, and then these people who were staying at the hangar were people against whom these criminal proceedings had already been initiated and they had already been convicted. There would people there whose sentences had already been pronounced by this court.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I see. So was that the case for the majority of the people there; in other words, that they had been convicted and were serving their sentences?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. In the other hangar on the other side -- actually, in the other two hangars, there were other people, people whose turn had not come yet for criminal proceedings to be initiated. So in this hangar, there were only people against whom criminal proceedings had been initiated and had been completed. I know two of them: Bahrija Begic and the other one is Suljic, I think, Jadrenko. They had already had sentences pronounced; five, six, seven years of imprisonment, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I understand now, Mr. Salkic. Thank you. What I want to know is this: I take it from your answer, there were three hangars, one of which kept sentenced prisoners, and were you in that one; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but also those against who proceedings were only initiated, whose proceedings were just underway.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. I understand. Thank you very much. Now, just one last question on the hangars. Were these three hangars all part of one complex, or were they widely separated, different parts of Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was at a big agricultural farm where they stored grain, so this was in one complex within one compound but at two different localities. They were about 150 to 200 metres from one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: After you had been to court, were you transferred from one of the hangars to this new hangar in which prisoners awaiting trial or serving sentences were kept?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was previously staying in one of the two hangars, and I was there only perhaps for an hour, an hour and a half, and then they took me to this court, where the proceedings had been initiated, and I did not return there any more. I went to the other hangar over there, where people who were already convicted were staying or people whose trials were underway.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in this hangar where people who had been convicted or who were awaiting trial, I'd like to you tell us what their ethnic background was and whether there were any soldiers or combatants amongst them, please.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were Muslims and Croats. There were only four or five officers of the former Yugoslav People's Army. As far as I could hear, they did not want to take part in the war, and they were detained together with us, and they had special treatment, different treatment from us. They were the only ones from who were in uniform. Actually, they were not in uniform. They were in civilian clothes. But they were addressing them in a different way, in such and such a way. They were not wearing uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you see -- just answer this next question with a yes or a no. You've told us that you saw Mr. Tadic on an occasion. Did you see him again at Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: How much time passed between you seeing him on the first occasion and the second occasion? Approximately, if you can't tell us precisely.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three to four days.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can you tell us if any of the prisoners in the hangar in which you now found yourself were doing any forced labour?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I don't want you to go into the detail, but can you give us an idea of how many, what sort of proportion of the prisoners were doing forced labour?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as forced labour is concerned, about 80 per cent of the people from this hangar went there, perhaps even 90 per cent of all the people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that you saw Mr. Tadic on this first occasion. I think you said that you saw him beyond the barbed wire. How long did you see him for? In other words, were you able to look at him for quite a long time, or was it just a glimpse as he passed by? Can you please tell us.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him only when passing by to the office of this warden, as we called him, the warden of this camp. It could have been about 15 metres or something like that. However, I did not see him throughout. I saw him quite well, very well, as a matter of fact, for about 10 metres or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Did you speak to him, or was it just a question of you seeing him and his walking on to wherever it was that he was going?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw him well, but I did not talk to him. I just saw him, that is to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like to ask you of the circumstances under which you next saw him. Was it in the same -- imprisoned in the same hangar?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, still.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And you've told us it was a matter of a few days later.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Tell us now how it was that you came to see him again on this second occasion, please.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is the way it was: A guard came. He called out our names. Those were the same names that were called out when they said who should not go to work that day. They took us out in front of this building where the warden's office was. That is to say, they took us out of the compound, or rather, beyond the wire. That was the second time that I saw Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And you were taken beyond the wire. What happened next?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then they searched all of us. They took away all the papers that we had from the court. They said that if anybody would hide such a paper, he could easily lose his life. So they took away all these papers. They didn't take the little bit of clothing we had. That is to say, that all the papers we had were taken away from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Now, I think you said on Friday that you managed to retain some papers. Are these the papers that you -- are these the sort of papers that were taken from the other prisoners but which you managed to somehow secrete and keep with you?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Approximately this could have been on the same day, in the afternoon hours. They searched the entire hangar, and they took other things from other people. I had a hunch that the same thing could happen, so then I took my shoe, lifted the insole, and I put this in. Since I had already had two hearings in court, there were lots of papers. And they did not look for this one particular paper. They didn't look at all of this in detail. So this first paper that said that criminal proceedings were being initiated against me, I managed to get that one out, and I took it out with me when I was exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can I ask you why you were keen to keep this paper? What significance did it hold for you?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it never occurred to me that it would be this kind of a court, but I thought that I should have some paper so that it would be known what kind of stupid things we were being charged with.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And is this the paper that you say can be faxed to us because it's at your home, faxed to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes. That's at my home right now. I had intended to take it here; however, since time was so short when I was about to leave, this wallet I have with telephone numbers, papers, my camp ID and things like that, it just stayed behind. So if necessary, I can ask them to fax this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: At some point did you ascertain that you were to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we had already got out, when they read out our names, actually, they already started saying that we were going to be exchanged. When we saw Mr. Tadic, we knew that he was involved in these exchanges, so even before it was announced, we knew that this was the group that would be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: How did you know that Mr. Tadic was involved in these exchanges? I'm not asking you about knowledge that you may have acquired since, but I'm asking you about the position back then, when you were in the camp. At that point in time, what was it that made you conclude that Mr. Tadic was involved in the exchanges? Think back to the time that you're standing there with your name being read out. What would have made you say then that Mr. Tadic was involved in the exchanges?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We all knew that Mr. Tadic was carrying out these exchanges, because he came earlier, and we heard about it. It was known from day one when these exchanges started that that is the way things were going involving this gentleman. I also heard this from others that there were other ways for people to get out, even if they would not be on the list. They told me about one particular man, and I had the opportunity of seeing that myself. If you ask me, perhaps I can explain that to you as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Will it provide us with insight as to why you say that Mr. Tadic was involved in carrying out the exchanges? If so, please tell us.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one occasion I saw in the camp my sister, whose name is Jasminka, Beba. She said that she went to see Mr. Tadic in order to see what the possibilities were for me going out on an exchange, because time had been going by and by. And he said that it would take a long time for me to get out. And that turned out to be true. It took 14 months for me to get out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Where did Jasminka see you?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was while I was still at the primary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: How did she manage to get in to see you?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it could happen when some of the guards would be, as we used to put it, very simply, a good man, and then a person could get in, not for a long time, for a minute or two, and you just ask, like, what the news was, whether somebody got killed or whether somebody was hurt or whatever. But we couldn't talk for very long. But she just told me this very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, can we go back to your -- Batkovic, please. Your name was read out. You realised that you were to be exchanged. Were you placed on buses?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They placed us on a truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry. And how many of you were placed on the truck?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for this exchange from Batkovic, there were 16 of us who had left then.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Batkovic, they transferred us to Samac. They practically drove us to Samac, where they detained us at the TO building again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. In the -- I'll withdraw that. Can you tell us what Mr. Tadic was doing during the course of the trip from Batkovic to Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't really say anything, because on the journey itself, I didn't see him any more. But he came to -- he came to Samac when we did, so he was probably in another car or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I see. Did you see him on -- upon your arrival in Samac?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Now, can you --

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He handed us over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you were taken into the TO building. Can you tell us of the sort of reception you received at the TO building on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not that we were received. You can't put it that way. You are just bringing in an inmate whose life is worthless. When you say "received," it makes me think of a very nice reception, when you are really making an effort about someone. However, I'll tell you what it was like. We came there around -- sometime during the day, and until 6.00 p.m., we did not have any problems whatsoever. And for about an hour, an hour and a half, we did not have any problems. That's what I'm trying to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: At the beginning of this trial, Mr. Salkic, you experienced some difficulties hearing. Do you have any hearing loss?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I have exceptionally good hearing. That is to say, I did have exceptionally good hearing. But from that 6.00 p.m. to 4.00 a.m. in the morning, my hearing was to suffer greatly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'd like you to tell the Court how it was -- what happened in that period of time, and in particular I'd like to you tell the Court how it was that your hearing suffered on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 6.00, perhaps a little later, Mr. Todorovic appeared with his entourage. There were five or six of them with him: Pop, Zvaka, Sole, and the old beaters. And Stevan ordered me to kneel down in front of him, which of course I had to do. He kicked me several times in my chest and stomach, and I remember him saying to the others that they shouldn't beat us in visible places because we would be up for the exchange. At one particular moment, Pop - that's what his nickname was, they called him Pop - came up to me from behind and hit me on the ears with the two palms of his hands, and from this compression, he broke my eardrums, and at the same time, he kicked me and I flew forward, I fell forward, and Mr. Todorovic proceeded to kick me. When he took aim for my stomach, he actually missed my stomach and hit me in the face, kicked me in the face, and I had a swelling and came to the actual spot for the exchange. I'll tell you about that later on. I fell by the line. But they beat us, four or five of us, and for one they used a bayonet, which they stabbed one of these young guys with, the two guys were from Rijeka in Croatia. They beat us unbearably. We couldn't take it any more. And I think that Mr. Tadic will confirm this: He called me out for an interview, probably with his superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'll get on to that interview in -- that you mentioned in due course. Were you removed from the TO the next morning, or the next day?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From there, we got into the buses and set out to the spot where the exchange was supposed to take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Would Your Honours just bear with me for a moment while I confer with my colleagues?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, I may be referring to the Times map, and I regret to say I've forgotten the exhibit number of it, the large map which is behind us. But I'd like to have a brief look at it before I do use it, if I use it. Might I ask that my colleague, Mr. Weiner, be permitted to go and get the map while I continue so we don't lose any time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, that's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Now, you said that you got onto buses and set out for the spot where the exchange would take place. Did you -- at that point in time, did you see Mr. Tadic, at about the time that you were loading onto the buses and getting ready to start the journey?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In front of the SUP and the TO, I didn't see him, because there was a crowd. There were a lot of people there, civilians, Muslims, and Croats who had stayed on, so that we were looking to see whether we'd see any people we knew of our families or relatives or something like that. So they didn't really need to make any lists or call out names.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Do I take it that there were others who were exchanged with you but who did not appear to have been imprisoned or incarcerated, as you and your fellow prisoners had been?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Standing around the buses, there were Muslims and Croats who had not been incarcerated, who -- those who were ready and prepared for the exchange were somewhere else, and they were loaded up onto the buses. We couldn't see that, nor did we know. So the people there were Muslims and Croats who were still free, moving around town.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did they have -- did the people who were obviously civilians and who hadn't been in prison but who were to be exchanged have their possessions with them, little suitcases and so on?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, those two buses stopped at the village of Crkvina, and that is about 4 kilometres away from Samac, and they would take them in with their belongings into that village hall, as we referred to it, whereas us detainees were separated to the right, and they searched all our belongings. And if anybody had any valuables or money, they were confiscated, but they had nothing to confiscate from us any more because we had moved around and they'd already done that. But nonetheless, they did search us all, but didn't find anything, no valuables. No valuables left on us. I heard that jewellery, money, gold, valuables were taken away, anybody who had taken these things when they went for the exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What was the purpose in stopping at Crkvina? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said for the search.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. I see.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To see if anybody had anything left over and if they did, to confiscate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you see any of the civilians - those who had some belongings with them - being searched?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were taken there. Some were crying and said -- everybody said, "They'd taken everything that we had left. I'm going into the world now, and I have nothing left with me." So there was just 10 metres between us and them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you -- I'll withdraw that question. How many buses all together were involved in this particular exchange?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two buses, but they were so full, so crammed, jam-packed. There were 150, 160, maybe 170 people in them. I can't give you an exact figure, but lots.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And where were you taken after Crkvina?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Crkvina we got into the buses again, and they took us off in the direction of Modrica, some 50 kilometres, where the road goes on to Derventa, and we continued in the direction of Banja Luka. However, we didn't take the left turning to Banja Luka; we went right towards Gradiska. And nearby, there's a place called Dragalic, which is where the exchange would take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Where is Dragalic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragalic is not far from Gradiska, in the neighbouring republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, might I ask, with the Court's permission, that the Times map be placed on the easel just briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, and then we can check whether it has an Exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It's P15, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm grateful to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Mr. Salkic, could I ask you just to stand up and see if you can point out -- see if you can find Dragalic or Dragalici - I'm not sure how you pronounce it - and then point it out to us.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please? I had taken off my headset.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Mr. Salkic, could you please have a look at the map and see if you can locate either the town or village of Dragalic; and if you can't find it, try and find the area in which it's located, in any event. Okay?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Get close to the map and have a good old look and tell us if you can find it.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be in this area here, this section between Okucani and Gradiska.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: May I approach the map itself and have a look myself, if Your Honours please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is Nova Gradiska, and Okucani is here. This is the cross. We were exchanged between Okucani and Gradiska on the motorway.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, the witness is indicating an area on the map near Nova Gradiska, in Croatia, and I think that should be sufficient for the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: The precise location is not a matter of great significance for the Prosecution, but it's inside Croatia and it's in that vicinity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Salkic. Resume your seat, please. All right. Now, you told us that you were taken there. Tell us how events unfolded after you had arrived at the exchange point.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it seemed to go on forever, a whole year, but actually, it was one or two hours. But it seemed to be eternal. And there were even rumours that the exchange wouldn't actually take place, which made us even more nervous. But nonetheless, the exchange did take place eventually. The people crossed over to one side and the others came over to the other side. And when I was saying goodbye to my friends - they didn't let us say goodbye while we were in the bus. I was saying goodbye to the civilians - Mr. Tadic at one point came and stood next to me and asked me to have a talk with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What did he say?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that he had been sent by a superior of his, a high-ranking superior from the 1st Corps, or the 5th Corps perhaps, Banja Luka corps, and that he wanted to see me and hear who had done what they had done to my face. And I answered in the affirmative. I said yes, I wanted to tell them who had done it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Anyway, all this was taking place at the petrol pump, and he took me over to the man who wanted to see me. He looked at me, and I looked at him, and he asked him, "Miro, who did this to this man?" Miro told me to say who it was, and I said that it was Stevan Todorovic, such-and-such, and that he had done such-and-such a thing to me. And at that point, a man from Batkovici interfered, somebody who was the chief or the security chief or something like that. He interrupted and he told Tadic, "Miro, I didn't give you people like this. I gave you people who were perfectly in order. They were in a proper state." And I know that he said to Tadic, "Miro, you can come to Batkovic in future, just bringing a list of people for the time and place of the exchange. I'm not going to give you any more people for them to end up looking like this man here." And I remember very well that Mr. Tadic said to him, "Well, it's not my fault," he said. And I went away from there. I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you succeed in crossing over the war lines and getting into Croatia?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was the section of Croatia that was under UNPROFOR's control, and that's where the exchange took place. We got into the buses and were driven off towards Zupanja, Orasje. And between Zupanja and Orasje, we crossed the river Sava, which is the border between Croatia and Bosnia, in fact, and I reached the village of Domalja [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Which village? The name of the village, please, the full name of the village.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Domaljevac. Domaljevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And is that now in the Federation part of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And is that just a matter of some kilometres down the road from Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Before the war, the village belonged to the Samac municipality. It is just 12 kilometres from Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Is that where you now live?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I live even closer to Samac, also in the Federation. The village is called Grebnice where I live.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And did you remain in that area, in Domaljevac and Grebnice, in the years following your release? Basically, have you been in that area ever since?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was there -- actually, I was on the battlefront until my wife and two children arrived, and they too had spent seven whole months in a camp --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and they were exchanged. The camp was called Zasovica. That's also a Croatian village which was completely emptied of Croats, and later on they set up a camp for Muslims and Croats there at that spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: How far from Bosanski Samac is Zasovica?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 5 kilometres, 6 at the most, going into the actual village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Would the Chamber just bear with me for one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And if Your Honours please, I'd just like the witness to point out to the Chamber the small village of Zasovica. You can see that on the map of Bosanski Samac and environs. Again, I regret to say I just don't have the -- my colleague tells me it's Exhibit P9. It's the map of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If it could just be quickly placed on the ELMO, we can identify where Zasavica is -- Zasovica, I should say.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can you just point out to Their Honours where one can see the village of Zasovica?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you move from Samac on the Samac-Modrica road, you turn off the road and there is a small bridge, and that's where the village of Zasovica is located.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Usher. I've finished with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You indicated where it was shown on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, it's marked on the map, so we don't need to mark it or anything like that, if Your Honours please, but for purposes of the transcript, the witness did identify that the village of Zasovica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Now, I know that you weren't there at Zasovica, and I know you have no direct knowledge of what the place was, but from anything that you have heard, can you tell us who was kept there, who was imprisoned there?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And my wife spent a lot of time there. You have already heard that my daughter was three and a half and seven months, actually, when she was incarcerated. My son was already 12 years old. My wife -- that is to say, the children had only just been born, some of them. I don't know whether there were those who had -- who were actually babies. There were quite a bit of elderly people too, who I heard had died from -- of old age, and that was the last few moments of their lives. And they all went to do forced labour. For my wife, I can guarantee that because she told me about it. When they took them to Odzak, they had them loot the houses and factories and work on the factory farms, to pick plums for slivovitz and pick the maize, the corn, and the kinds of physical labour that she had never done before.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can you tell us - and again I know it's only from what you have heard - who was imprisoned there? By that, I mean the ages of people who were imprisoned there and the sex of people who were imprisoned there, if there was anything in particular as far as those features are concerned.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is how it was. There were Muslims and Croats. Nobody else was shut up there. There were women and there were children, as well as elderly people. Able-bodied -- there were no able-bodied men there because if they wanted to incarcerate an able-bodied man, then he was with us in the camp we were in, where they kept us men.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you also said that you saw action after your release. Where did you fight?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. I was in the Croatian Defence Council. That's where I spent - and I can give you the exact date too - up until 1994. And when my wife was exchanged, that was then - and I was to hear about this from her - she was exchanged on the other side of the Federation, where the Muslims and Croats were at war, so that she was not able to come in this circuitous route to meet up with me. I didn't see her for two years -- actually, two years minus 16 days, 16 days less than two years.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: How old was your child, your daughter, I should say, when you were arrested? How old was she when you were reunited with her?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was three years and two months old. She was a little, little girl. And my son was barely 11. When we met up, he was a different child altogether by that time, and when he saw me for the first time, he said to me, "Daddy, you're not as fat as you used to be." I don't want to talk about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Now, I just need to ask you a few more questions, and then I'll be finished asking you questions, Mr. Salkic.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Up until the time that your name was read out on a list by Mr. -- by Mr. Tadic, did you have any input, any influence, any say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, objection, a leading question. The witness did not say that Tadic had read out any kind of list.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'll say this ten times if I need to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I think Mr. Krgovic's objection is -- may be correct. I apologise if I led the witness. I didn't mean to. But I'll set matters straight with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Mr. Salkic, I just want to know about the list. You mentioned it already briefly. I assumed somebody read it out. Can you tell us who in fact did read out the list of the names, of the 16 names of the men who were to be exchanged from Batkovic.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, loading us up into that truck, in order to take us off to Samac, Mr. Tadic read out 16 names. And I can repeat some of them, because it's a sort of new birthday; you remember those things. I don't remember my birthday or celebrate my birthday any more but that, I do. There was Mr. Nalic, Tihic, Salkic, Tihic, Zaimbegovic, and many, many others.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That list was read out by Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what I was leading to was this: At the time that that list was read out to you and you were loaded up into the truck, had you had any say or input or participated in the decision of whether or not you would be exchanged? Now, it may seem perfectly obvious to you, but I want to know. Tell us.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me answer that. After all the suffering that one went through, it would be -- I don't know which term to use, but it wouldn't -- it would not be fitting to ask somebody whether they wanted to or not. It was the only way to save my head. There was no other solution for me but to be exchanged. However, on one occasion, actually that night when they beat us - and I forgot to say this, so let me take advantage and let the Trial Chamber know - when Mr. Todorovic beat me, he -- as I was lying down, bending down to kiss his feet, he put his leg on my neck and said, "Don't you dare come back from the exchange, from the delineation line and come back." And I said, "Well, I never -- it would never enter into my head to come back after that."

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Before you were arrested in April 1992, did you have any plans or intention of leaving your home and the town in which you'd lived in all your life?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several months before, I bought the video games, I invested my money, and for the -- those times, it was a lot of money. Maybe it's not much money for here, but at the time it was a lot of money. And my friends, the Serbs, said that there would be a war coming and that I shouldn't invest, that I should wait and see, and I said, "I'm sure it won't come to that." And never, under any normal circumstances, would I have left my own town had there not been a war, because that's where all my family is buried, all my forefathers, in the cemetery there. My son is buried there. All my family is there. That's where I was born. And quite certainly, quite certainly, I would never have left it of my own free will.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: When you were taken in the bus and you finally arrived at Dragalic, did you have anything given to you by any authority, a soldier, a civilian, a bureaucrat, anyone, indicating the property that you had left behind, the video -- the little video store and the kombi van and your workshop and your tools and all that sort of stuff? Did you have anything to prove that you were the owner, or to compensate you for that property?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: We don't have a translation over here. I don't know about you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Neither did we get any.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Mr. Salkic, I'll repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear us now? Because something went wrong in all the interpretation booths.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Mr. Salkic, there was a bit of a problem with the interpretation. I'll ask the question again. When you were handed over at Dragalic, when you were exchanged, did you have anything from anyone at all proving or attesting to your ownership of property that you'd left behind in Bosanski Samac, things like your kombi van, your workshop, your wife's video store, your apartment, things like that? Or, indeed, had you been given anything that would enable you to receive compensation for the taking of that property?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. No certificate, no document. I didn't get anything from anyone. And I didn't hear of anyone else having gotten anything either.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Were you aware of anyone else who was being exchanged who was given such documentation or compensated?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I did not hear of any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And the last topic that I'd like to just ask you about briefly, Mr. Salkic, is this: You have described injuries that you received, the hearing, hearing loss. Have you had that tested?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Are you ever going to get your hearing back to the levels it was before you were attacked and assaulted?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. It is no longer possible, except through some kind of expensive surgery, and I haven't got the money for that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just one question, Your Honours. What is our schedule for this afternoon? Do we have a break in half an hour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We shall have a break at 1630 and then resume at 1700 hours to 1830.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Salkic, I am Pantelic, attorney at law, for Mr. Blagoje Simic. If you're upset because of all of this, please tell the Trial Chamber, and if you'd like a break, I'm sure that things could be arranged.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how much time is left until we actually have the break. I guess I won't mind. Could you just tell me what time it is and how much time we have left?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It is five past 4.00 now, and we'd be working until 4.30.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. I can manage that, and thank you for having asked me this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Salkic, you gave two statements to the Office of the Prosecutor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, but according to my records, I have one statement from the 7th and 9th of February, 1995. Do you remember that statement?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please speak up a bit? I really have trouble hearing you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness also speak into the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can the usher assist the witness, please, to come closer to the microphone, and also increase the volume for the earphones.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Salkic, I have here before me a statement that you gave on the 7th and 9th of February. You gave it to the OTP. Do you remember that statement?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which year?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The second statement that I have in my records was given on the 10th of March, 1998. Do you remember that one? That's shorter than the first one.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But I haven't got the third statement. Can you help me with that? When did you give this third statement?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I don't know, so you can talk to your colleague about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. [In English] Please, if my learned colleague can clarify this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe we can have clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I don't know what third statement Mr. Pantelic is talking about. I know that we disclosed notes of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. It's the witness who mentioned that he made three statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Sorry. My apologies. I don't know what statement the witness is talking about. I know that we disclosed notes of certain conversations we had with this witness to the Defence, and that related to conversations we had with this witness in July of this year. But they were notes, our notes, that we disclosed to the Defence. They weren't reviewed or signed by the witness, and in that sense they're not classical statement. But I don't know if that's of assistance to Mr. Pantelic or not, but that's the situation that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: -- as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So that's the situation with the Prosecution. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So that was sometime in July this year, as the Prosecutor had put it. Actually, it wasn't a statement; it was probably just an interview or conversation with you.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That's the way I considered it. I'm not really very good at writing and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I understand that. Thank you. Mr. Salkic, please, it seems to me there is some kind of a misunderstanding because so much time has gone by. As far as I can remember, before this Trial Chamber you said that in Bijeljina there was a certain judge, Goran Blagojevic, who said to you that it's not important what kind of sentence you're going to get; it's important for you to go for an exchange. Do you remember having said that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but he was not the one who was trying me. The judge, that same man, was my friend before the war, during the war, and he's still my friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That is the point. We should clarify things here, because in your statement you said that on one occasion Mirko Vasiljevic, president of the court, walked in, and Predrag Drinic, a judge, is that correct, and then they said that to you.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't you tell me what they said. You asked me what they said, and I'll tell you, not what you say that I said that they said to me. I don't agree with you on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead. Tell us.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In one room, that I described very nicely, I was talking to Mr. Goran Blagojevic, and Goran Blagojevic said this to me. And in the hallway I met these two gentlemen. I also said hello to them, we greeted each other, and there wasn't much that was said, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please read this section to me from your statement, the one that I have marked, and then give me a comment in terms of that. Was that statement correct or this, what you have been saying now?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Statement of 7th and 9 February 1995, ERN number -- this is B/C/S version. ERN number is 00637760. Unfortunately, I don't have a paging in this copy, but the ERN number is that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please read slowly for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see this. We were standing in the hallway, and they were walking through this hallway. Yes. So you'd think it's just words. Then Mirko Vasiljevic, president of the court, and Predrag Drinic, a judge, walked in. They greeted me nicely, because we knew each other from before. They said to me the higher the sentence was, it would be better, because I would be exchanged earlier. Yes, yes, but that's not the way it had been put. Goran said that to me, and I saw these two men in court. So I'll read this on, and then I'll make further comments: "I told them about the beating and they issued orders to the effect that this should not take place. Two days later Goran called me and said to me that it would be best if they would return me to Batkovici again." How come? How could Goran call me? I know there are going to be questions in this regard. "It would be best if they would return me to Batkovic again. That's what happened. And I was travelling in a van with markings of the new Yugoslav army, and I would see --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Salkic, can you read slowly, because the interpreters have to interpret in the language we understand.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I don't know where they stopped with the interpretation, but I'll proceed: "This happened. I was travelling in a van with markings -- insignia of the new Yugoslav army, the JA. I frequently saw troops of a Serbian corps, Vlasenica and Valjevo Corps, in January and February 1993. The corps had been stationed near Vlasenica for a while."

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Salkic, if I understood that statement correctly, it is contrary to what you have just explained to us. So basically, you abide by the version you just gave to the Trial Chamber, that this is not the most fortunate of versions of what you just said.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please pause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Mr. Salkic, because you are speaking the same language with counsel, you should remember that the interpreters have to interpret what counsel has said before you can answer, so please do pause. Can you start your answer again?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Salkic, please tell us about this event slowly.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Should I describe it in detail?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, no, just in principal.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The guard brought us -- brought me into Mr. Blagojevic's office. He had asked to see me. He knocked at the door, and he said, "Captain, I have brought this man," and now, not to go into all the details, taking off my handcuffs and things like that. I walked in. He said what he said to me. Mr. Blagojevic said it. It was not Vasiljevic and the other one. However, this is probably some kind of confusion. I don't know. But I got out of the office, and then -- and then Mr. Mirko Vasiljevic and Predrag Drinic walked into the hallway from the stairs. We greeted each other, and of course we exchanged a few words, but they did not say this to me. It was only Mr. Blagojevic who said it. And then I was taken to the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I please get this back? Thank you. Precisely. So that was the objective, for us to clarify these two versions that are different. You see, Mr. Salkic, when reading your statement from 1995, I came to the conclusion that you did not go into detail with regard to your transport from Bijeljina to Samac. You spoke about this in a bit more detail before this Trial Chamber. So please, could you just give answers to a few more questions so that we could clarify this particular matter as well. When you arrived on that bus from Bijeljina via Loncari to Samac - I'm talking about the 13th of May - can you tell us: When you got into Samac, where did you exactly stop with this bus? Where did they drive you to with that bus?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We stopped in front of the hall of the secondary school, right in front of it, and then we got off.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned a few names, a few persons, actually, who were with you at the time. Can you tell me whether Mr. Izet Izetbegovic was with you?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Was Mr. Muhamed with you, and his brother, Hasan Bicic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: On the bus, was there somebody else from Samac whom you knew from before?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all of us, except for those who were added to our group.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But please give me a few names.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can give you names. [redacted]; Bicic, Muhamed; Bicic, Muhamed; Bikic, Ames; Tabakovic, Sulejman; [redacted]. And now give me time and I will write the names of all 60-odd people for you, but just give me enough time to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: This is quite sufficient. Thank you. While looking through your statement from 1995, not in a single place did I find the event that you described when Stevan Todorovic, as you said, when Blagoje Simic came to the gym. Did you not remember it at the time, or was there some other reason why you didn't say this in 1995?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps it wasn't necessary for me to remember it. However, when you see that these details are being requested, then I did remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You mean requested by the Office of the Prosecutor to explain that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah, don't be so provocative. Please don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Salkic, counsel is asking questions because he has a duty to do so. He is defending his client, Mr. Blagoje Simic. And the Trial Chamber has allowed him to cross-examine you. The Trial Chamber is also searching for the truth, so on the other hand, counsel is also asking for these details on behalf of the Trial Chamber, so please be polite to counsel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would also ask him at the same time not to answer these questions -- I mean not to put questions like this to me, like, "You did say this or you did do this, didn't you?" I imagine he should just put a question to me, rather than giving the answer as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no. He -- at the moment, he has the statements which were recorded by the Prosecution. The statements were from you. Now, he is entitled put the contents of the statements to you. Now, if what is your statement is not correct, it's not because Mr. Pantelic is quoting the wrong thing. So you simply explain why there are differences between the evidence you've given in court and the contents of your statement which you gave to the Prosecution. Perhaps it would help if counsel -- if when you want to quote what is in the statement you specifically say, "In this paragraph, in this line of your statement," and then counsel reads that. Then it will be clearer, I think, to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Madam President. That is the situation. In this statement, as I said, which is around 11 pages, I didn't find any mention, any reference to name of my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. So you asked --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I don't know how to ask negative questions, so I put him this question. I reviewed this statement. There is no mention of my client. And now he said, "Okay, it wasn't mentioned but someone asked me." And I simply want to know who asks him and when.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I think I explained to the witness. I'm sure from now on we will have no problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Salkic, since you did not mention Mr. Blagoje Simic at all in your statement from 1995, and you probably talked to the Prosecutor in preparation of this trial, and the Prosecutor probably put some questions to you, did he then ask you about this detail concerning the presence of Mr. Blagoje Simic in this gym?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not ask me about this detail. I told him about that detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Usher, please, your assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Salkic in your statement from the 10th of March, 1998 --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The B/C/S version of the statement of March 10, 1998, ER number is 00637103, page number 3, paragraph 6. Paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Salkic, there is a sentence here in your statement from 1998. Please read it. Just read it out to me, please. I've marked it with the magic marker. Just the sentence that I marked please.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I'll read it to you with pleasure.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Please just read it.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "During the war, I did not see Blagoje Simic."

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all I wanted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: However, that was when I gave my first statement and --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll ask you about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have a number for that statement? Identification only?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Actually, Madam President, I don't know if you want to put all these statements, but this is the extract.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You are through? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: There is no -- I think my learned friend will not object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's a part of the statement, and it's in transcript now, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Salkic, please, could you briefly sketch out the gym for me, with the entrance, the entrance hall as well. If you would please be so kind as to do that. We are talking about this particular event now, so I just need a very, very basic sketch, just the entrance and the gym, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Which one --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Madam President, gym of secondary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: If maybe you have a magic marker which is a little bit better. The other one, I think. No, no, the black one. That one is better.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Salkic, please, before you put it -- or actually, if it's easier for you, perhaps you can mark it there directly. This arrow, that is the entrance into the school, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the entrance into the school. This is the gym, this. This is the gym, "s-a-l-a."

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you. And the entrance into the gym is this part, isn't it? Could you just mark it with a small arrow?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the entrance. I'll mark it. I'll mark the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could you please mark in this gym, with little crosses, your own position, where you were.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And could you please put the letter "A" there.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So this is the reference to the position of the witness with the letter "A."

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please now put another "X" in the place where Hasan Bicic was, or if you know someone else who was with you.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you how people were standing, but you're asking me for a lot now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Right. How they were standing.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Through the gym, this way. Now, not to give them all numbers. We were all around there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. So we are stating that practically all the detainees were lined up round the walls?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And tell me now, since Stiv Todorovic appeared at the door, could you please mark Stiv Todorovic with an "X" as well.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: There?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Would you mark him with a number "1."

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And where was Blagoje Simic standing?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here at that door, too, a bit further away. First Stiv walked in, looked through the gym. Since the door is a bit narrower than the usual double door but it is still wider than a usual door, Stiv withdrew there and Blagoje remained there with his body at the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could you please mark Blagoje with number"2."

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And I think, Your Honours, it's time for a break. Probably I'm finished but several questions, I would have to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Could we have a number for this sketch, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, can we have a number? The title can be, "The sketch of Mr. Ibrahim Salkic of the secondary school gym."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Just wait for the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number will be D19/1 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Salkic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We shall adjourn now and resume our proceedings at 1700 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Cross-examination continues. Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Madam President. Just a couple of questions and I'm done with my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Salkic, you mentioned the fact that there were several other people with these two, Blagoje and Stivo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Does the name Srecko Radovanovic ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And how about the nickname Debeli?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we called Osman Semso, in Samac, Debeli, but I don't know anybody else nicknamed Debeli, or "fat," in translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You didn't know any of the members of the paramilitary units or policemen whose nickname was Debeli?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Salkic. [In English] I've finished my cross-examination. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The next counsel. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Salkic.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you too. Well, it's already evening, but anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Salkic, I'm going to ask you a few questions, and I should like to ask you, if possible, to answer with "yes" or "no" or "I don't know."

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Salkic, you were born in Bosanski Samac; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And your father's name was Meho; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You served the army -- did your military service in the navy between 1973 to 1975, is that right, 21st of March, 1975, in fact?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You were trained in anti-sabotage activities in the army; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can give you the exact branch. It was the mine and anti-mine unit, and it meant laying mines on the seabed and to dismantle them afterwards on ships.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So this mine and anti-mine training was your specialty?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, but in the navy, to do with ships.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I see. So mine and anti-mine training for ships.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You testified before this Tribunal, Mr. Salkic, and said that as a hunter, you possessed two hunting rifles, I believe. One was a carbine; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And you also said that you procured a Kalashnikov.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean hunting weapons?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, but that you procured a Kalashnikov; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your friends Hasan and Muhamed also procured a Kalashnikov each; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let them tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether you know about that.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mr. Salkic, on page -- on a page of the transcript of the 1st of November, the number of the page is 3208 and 3209, line 25 and the second and third line, you confirmed, asked by the Prosecutor, that you procured the weapons illegally; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, just the Kalashnikov, but I had the licences for my hunting rifles. That was in order.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I see. Thank you. But I was thinking of the Kalashnikov. You have been a hunter for many years?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I'm still a hunter today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: As a seasoned hunter, I'm sure you know about the provisions relating to the possession of firearms that were in force in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sure you also know that on the basis of those rules and regulations, it was -- you were not allowed to possess military weapons such as Kalashnikovs. You know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You are also aware of the fact that the law provided that the possession and harbouring of, and carrying of, illegal firearms, and especially automatic weapons, was a crime?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, that law was no longer in force. It didn't exist because Yugoslavia didn't exist any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the laws that were in force in Bosnia-Herzegovina before April 1992.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I saw that others had these zolja type of weapons from the 4th Detachment, and Kalashnikovs. Why shouldn't I buy some? If they were allowed to, why shouldn't I be permitted to do the same?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I should just like you to answer my question. I understand you completely, but please limit yourself to my questions and answering them, to facilitate the work of the Trial Chamber and all of us present in the courtroom. Thank you. So if I understood you correctly, you were aware of that, you did know the law?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Salkic, you testified here before this Trial Chamber and said Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that you were not a member of any form of armed formation of the SDA before April 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Could the usher please help me with something? Could these documents be marked for identification, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit, Defence Exhibit D8/2 ter ID and D8/2 ID.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, the original to Mr. Salkic, and the one on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Salkic can you see the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Would you read out, please, the left-hand corner, what it says there? Where it says number "2," what does it say after that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Anti-sabotage section."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And underneath that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "KD," which is probably "Commander," Husein Arapovic, aka Arap, and the telephone number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know Mr. Husein Arapovic, nicknamed Arap?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, tell me -- no, I withdraw that question. Mr. Husein Arapovic, was he a member of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Would you please read out what it says under number "7."

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My name is there, comes to be there, but I don't know how. Ibrahim Salkic, aka "Ibala." I'm not Ibala. I'm Ibela, with an "E."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Ibela is your nickname, is it?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Ibela, and not Ibala. I-b-e-l-a and not I-b-a-l-a.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So you're saying that it's Ibela?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So under that number, that is your name next to the number, is it?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, the five numbers that follow, 63238 --

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my former telephone number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- that was your telephone number in April 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I tell a lie. Yes, I did see it in the SUP, in Bosanski Samac, when the war began.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You mean when you gave your statements?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not before that. I didn't see it before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You were shown the document on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the first time I saw it in my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mr. Salkic, who else from this list that you have before you was incarcerated with you, first in the Territorial Defence building and then in the primary school building?
